title: Summit and Escarpment
premise: Silas Sterling, a railroad engineer who keeps to herself and her maps of closed mountain lines, discovers a tide-revealed cave holding the remains of a survey party that vanished forty years ago—including evidence that her own grandfather falsified the route that doomed them. When word leaks and treasure hunters descend on the valley, Silas must cross the escarpment ahead of the first snows to reach the old summit depot and destroy the records before they ruin what's left of her family name. Pursued by a ruthless collector who wants the map intact, she survives an avalanche, betrayal, and her own guilt, learning that survival means carrying memory rather than erasing it. In the end she reaches the depot, chooses truth over secrecy by publishing the corrected route, and finds belonging in the mountain town she'd always kept at arm's length.
about_author: O. M. Sterling is the pen name of a former surveyor's assistant who spent a decade mapping decommissioned rail lines across the northern ranges before turning to fiction. They write from a cabin near the timberline, where the winters are long enough for exactly one book apiece.

chapters.title: The Map of Closed Lines
chapters.summary: Silas Sterling, POV. A railroad engineer living alone above a fading mountain town, Silas catalogs abandoned rail lines no one else remembers. Her careful invisibility is established alongside her obsessive inheritance: her grandfather's survey maps. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for safety.

chapters.title: What the Tide Uncovered
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. An extreme low tide exposes a sea cave below the escarpment; inside she finds a rusted strongbox from the lost 1911 survey party—her grandfather's colleagues. Among the effects: a letter accusing someone of altering the route. Emotional beat: dread blooming into compulsion.

chapters.title: The Letter in the Tin
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She deciphers the water-damaged letter naming 'S.S.' as the man who moved the line. Confronting her family's legend, she burns nothing and tells no one—but a local fisherman saw her at the cave. Emotional beat: guilt as inheritance.

chapters.title: Word Travels Downhill
chapters.summary: Tomas Reyes, POV. The fisherman sells his story to a visiting antiquities dealer, Edmund Voss, who arrives asking questions about the 1911 party. Tomas, uneasy but tempted by money, points Voss toward Silas's cabin. Emotional beat: small betrayals compound like snowfall.

chapters.title: The Collector
chapters.summary: Voss, POV. Charming and ruthless, Voss interviews townsfolk and reconstructs the cave's location. He believes the original route map survived and is worth a fortune—and he doesn't care whose name it blackens. Emotional beat: menace wearing a polite face.

chapters.title: Questions at the Door
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Voss visits under scholarly pretenses; Silas lies badly about the strongbox. Afterward she realizes the only way to control the story is to reach the summit depot first, where her grandfather's true field notes are stored. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Provisions and Lies
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She quietly buys supplies, telling the storekeeper she's inspecting culverts. Old friend Ruthie Kettle sees through her and extracts a promise: come back alive, and come back honest. Emotional beat: the cost of being known.

chapters.title: First Ascent
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She enters the closed line through a collapsed tunnel, testing trestles and remembering her grandfather teaching her to read grade and curve. Flashbacks deepen his character—brilliant, ambitious, afraid. Emotional beat: love and anger entwined.

chapters.title: The Washout
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. A section of roadbed gives way; she nearly dies crossing a gorge and loses half her food. From the ridge she spots a second party on the line behind her—Voss has hired guides. Emotional beat: the wilderness forgives nothing.

chapters.title: Company on the Line
chapters.summary: One of Voss's guides, Ilsa Brandt, POV. Ilsa, a former army mountaineer with debts, begins doubting Voss's methods when he orders them to cut switchbacks and leave markers that will mislead rescue parties. Emotional beat: conscience stirring under pressure.

chapters.title: The Way Station
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Sheltering in a derelict way station, she finds carved initials of the 1911 party and a child's tin whistle—one survivor was a boy. She realizes the boy lived and grew up somewhere, unnamed. Emotional beat: history becoming personal.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Ruthie, POV. In town, Voss pressures the sheriff to declare Silas trespassing; Ruthie stalls him and sends a warning up-line via the telegraph remnant at the pass. Emotional beat: loyalty as quiet defiance.

chapters.title: Whiteout
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Early snow catches her on the exposed shoulder of the escarpment. She holes up for two days, rationing, hallucinating her grandfather's voice. She confronts him aloud—anger finally spoken. Emotional beat: grief given weather.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Switchback
chapters.summary: Ilsa, POV. Ordered to intercept Silas, Ilsa instead warns her off the main line and takes a beating from Voss's other guide for it. Silas escapes east onto the dangerous high traverse. Emotional beat: an enemy choosing a side.

chapters.title: The High Traverse
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. The traverse tests everything she knows: cornices, deadman anchors, a night spent belayed to a rusted rail. She stops running from the past and starts planning how to tell the whole truth. Emotional beat: endurance becoming purpose.

chapters.title: What Voss Wants
chapters.summary: Voss, POV. Closing in, Voss reveals his motive to Ilsa: his grandfather was the 1911 party's leader, blamed for the disaster. He doesn't want money—he wants vindication, even if it means destroying Silas's family instead. Emotional beat: mirrored wounds.

chapters.title: The Summit Depot
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She reaches the depot and unlocks her grandfather's cache: field notes proving he altered the route under pressure from investors, then spent his life paying anonymous settlements to the victims' families—including Voss's. Emotional beat: the full weight of the price of survival.

chapters.title: Confrontation Above the Clouds
chapters.summary: Silas and Voss, alternating. Voss arrives; they argue amid the storm while the depot's roof groans under snowload. Silas offers him the notes—not destruction, not sale, but the truth entire. He wavers; the roof begins to fail. Emotional beat: vengeance meeting honesty.

chapters.title: Avalanche
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. The slope cuts loose. Silas and Voss shelter inside the depot's stone vault as the building shreds around them; the notes are nearly lost and saved together. Buried, waiting, they speak plainly for the first time. Emotional beat: shared mortality dissolving enmity.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Silas and Ilsa, POV. Digging out at dawn, the three begin the descent, Ilsa having turned back Voss's remaining hired men. The mountain is silent, scoured, indifferent. Emotional beat: exhaustion, gratitude, the strange peace after survival.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Back in town, Silas publishes the corrected route and the full account of 1911, accepting her grandfather's guilt and honoring the dead by name—including the boy who survived, now an old man who writes to thank her. Emotional beat: memory chosen over myth.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Spring. Silas takes a post maintaining the reopened line, teaches Ruthie's students to read maps, and hangs the tin whistle by her door. Invisible no longer, and no longer alone. Emotional beat: home as something built, not found.
